document_title: Three Yeas, Three Short, No Start Date
post_copy:
On the Alaska Senate floor in Juneau on May 16th, data center bill SB 250 passed 14 to 5.

The U.S. House passed H.R. 9340, a grid cost standard for big computing sites, 417 to 3 on September 16th. Begich voted yea.

Alaska's House held SB 250 in committee on May 18th. It went no further.

The U.S. Senate stopped at 57 on September 30th, with 60 needed for cloture. Murkowski and Sullivan voted yea.

Gold marks Alaska's three yeas in a 100-cup Senate tray at 57 and a 432-cup House tray at 417, beside two unturned sand-glasses, a three-bay exemption cabinet, SB 250's 14 and 5 and a steel rule with no enactment tick.

Each bill cleared one chamber. H.R. 9340 would waive its review deadlines for a state whose legislature voted on a comparable standard before an enactment that hasn't happened.

Does "the State legislature has voted" mean both chambers?

#SB250 #AKLeg #RatepayerProtectionAct

slides.headline: Alaska's three votes were yes. The Senate fell three short.
labels: MURKOWSKI YEA   SULLIVAN YEA   BEGICH YEA

slides.headline: Cloture needed 60. It got 57.
slides.body: Three-fifths of the Senate had to agree just to take it up. The motion was then withdrawn. Lisa Murkowski and Dan Sullivan both voted yea. The House had passed it two weeks before.
labels: "Cloture on the Motion to Proceed Rejected (57-43, 3/5 majority required)"

slides.headline: Two weeks earlier, the House passed it 417 to 3.
slides.body: Nick Begich voted yea. Republicans went 210 to 0, Democrats 206 to 3 and the one independent voted yea. Suspending the rules took two-thirds.
labels: "On Motion to Suspend the Rules and Pass, as Amended"

slides.headline: A standard for computing sites of 100 MW and up.
slides.body: Rates would be designed to recover that cost from the customer, even if it ends its contract. Each state regulator would have to consider the standard and decide.
labels: "the full, incremental cost of any generation, transmission, or distribution upgrade necessary"
100 MW OR MORE AT ONE SITE OR CAMPUS

slides.headline: Both clocks start on a day that hasn't happened.
labels: "Not later than 1 year after the date of enactment of this paragraph"

slides.headline: It also counts backward.
slides.body: A state skips both clocks if, before enactment, it had put a comparable standard in place, held a proceeding on one, or its legislature had voted on one. Has Alaska done any of the three?

slides.headline: Alaska's Senate passed SB 250, 14 to 5. A House panel held it.
slides.body: It passed May 16th and was heard and held in House Community and Regional Affairs two days later. Does one chamber's vote count as "the State legislature has voted"?

slides.headline: Every date on the record, and the one not set.
labels: SB 250 heard and held in House CRA

Date of enactment. Both clocks run from it.

editor_notes_for_email: This update of No.58 says all three of Alaska's members of Congress voted yea on H.R. 9340. Begich voted yea in the House's 417 to 3 on September 16th, and Murkowski and Sullivan voted yea in the Senate's 57 to 43 cloture vote on September 30th, three short of the 60 needed, after which the motion to proceed was withdrawn. The deck never calls the bill dead, never predicts the lame duck, never says whether Alaska is or isn't exempt, and leaves Schumer's "toothless" line out on purpose. The SB 250 tally and the RCA statute were read through a proxy because akleg.gov refuses automated reads, and the Alaska Beacon page returned 403 to the fact checker, so open the BASIS and Beacon links yourself before you post.
